articles.title: Israel kills six Palestinians in Gaza on eve of announcement of election results
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: The Israeli military intensified its deadly attacks on Palestinians in different parts of the Gaza Strip in the last 24 hours that preceded the announcement of the Knesset election results, which are expected by the morning of Friday, October 30. Read more: Israel’s elections: all roads lead to genocide At least six Palestinians were killed and dozens of others wounded in Israeli strikes that targeted different areas of the war-torn enclave. The fatalities include four government employees , who were killed in an Israeli strike on the Ministry of Economy in the Al-Mawasi area, west of the southern city of Rafah. Thirty others were wounded in the same offensive. The Gaza-based government media office condemned the assault in a statement published on Telegram, describing it as “a new crime and a horrific massacre that targeted a group of civilian public-sector employees.” It added that “targeting government teams and civilian public employees is part of the organized crime that the Israeli occupation has practiced, and a malicious exposed attempt to push towards chaos and disorder by undermining the work of government crews and institutions, which seek to maintain the stability and safety of society.” Meanwhile, two people were killed and several others were wounded when an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle near the entrance to the Al-Maghazi refugee camp, in the central Deir al-Balah Governorate. The latest deaths take the toll of people killed by Israel in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire deal was reached in October 2025 to more than 1,574 people, with 5,867 others wounded, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry also reported that at least 74,570 people have been killed since Israel started its genocidal aggression on the besieged strip in October 2023.

articles.title: The world once again calls for an end to the US blockade on Cuba
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Last Wednesday, October 28, the United Nations General Assembly voted (for the thirty-fourth time) in favor of ending the economic and commercial embargo – which many refer to as a blockade – that the United States has unilaterally imposed on Cuba for more than sixty years. With 130 votes in favor, 17 against, and 25 abstentions, the international community once again demanded that the United States end an embargo that has caused unimaginable hardship for the Cuban people and has slowed the Caribbean nation’s development. One of the countries that voted against the embargo was South Africa, whose ambassador emphasized his concern about the negative consequences the Cuban people are suffering as a result of Washington’s decisions. He also called for Cuba to be removed from the list of countries that allegedly sponsor terrorism, a designation that prevents many companies from doing business on the island. In recent years, the Cuban Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denounced that high-level US diplomats had pressured several of its partners to vote against such resolutions concerning the embargo on Cuba, under threat of serious consequences. The denunciation was repeated this year by Cuba’s top diplomat. Despite these efforts, the overwhelming majority of countries once again called on the United States to end the embargo. Washington appeared to have successfully influenced only its closest allies (those fully aligned with its geopolitical ideology) to vote against it. Thus, among the countries that voted against the resolution are several signatories to “Shield of the Americas,” the new international military initiative led by Washington, to which several right-wing and far-right governments in Latin America have aligned themselves. For its part, the UN news portal reported : “The Assembly expresses its concern that, after decades of votes and appeals, the measure remains in force and continues to negatively affect the Cuban population and Cuban nationals residing abroad, without the expectations of economic normalization having been met.” A multimillion-dollar blockade According to Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez , Cuba’s annual losses are estimated at about 8 billion dollars. The total economic losses since the embargo began amount to the astronomical figure of 178 billion dollars, which is a huge sum considering the relatively small size of a country with a population of 10 million. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez on October 28, showing a calculation of economic losses from the blockade since the UN debate began. Photo: Zoe Alexandra In this regard, the US economic and trade embargo – the longest-lasting in recent modern history – has been denounced by Cuban authorities as a perverse mechanism employed by Washington to boycott, almost from its inception, the Cuban Revolution, which proclaimed itself anti-imperialist and socialist. Added to this prolonged damage are the recent energy restrictions that Washington has imposed on Cuba. Since early 2026, when Washington targeted Venezuela (Cuba’s main energy partner), the possibility of sending oil to Cuba has been cut off by a unilateral US order; the United States warned it would increase tariffs on any country that sends crude oil to Cuba. Only one Russian tanker managed to navigate the waters and reach Cuba – a resource appreciated by Cubans but one that ran out quite quickly. The Caribbean nation depends almost entirely on petroleum for generating electricity, production, trade, and providing hospital care to its population. Added to this are the difficulties in distributing water and meeting other basic needs of the Cuban people, who are the true victims of a new strategy aimed at overthrowing the revolutionary government. In this regard, the support of the international community – the vast majority of which has called for an end to the embargo, considering it a measure that undermines the sovereignty and self-determination of the Cuban people – provides a platform to remind the world of the situation Cuba is facing. Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel said on X : “Today at the UN, the international community’s overwhelming support for Cuba was evident in its condemnation of the blockade and the US government’s policy of maximum pressure. Most of the speakers, some representing regional blocs, were clear in their condemnation.” He added : “It is a despicable act on the part of the empire’s representatives to claim they are defending collective punishment – which exacts a high human cost – against the Cuban people, in violation of human rights. It is a futile effort. They are not convincing, and they achieve nothing except through gangster-like coercion.” Exchange of accusations between Havana and Washington But the vote was not without controversy. During his address, the US representative to the UN, Mike Waltz, said that concentration camps existed in Cuba where “thousands of homosexuals, Christians, and Afro-Cubans” were allegedly detained. In response to the statement, the Cuban delegation, visibly upset, began banging on the table and requested a “point of order.” When the Assembly president did not respond, Foreign Minister Rodríguez and the rest of the Cuban delegation approached the presiding officers and Waltz and demanded that he stop lying. Cuban delegation calls for a point of order during US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz’s speech. Photo: Zoe Alexandra Following the protests, the Assembly president gave the floor to Rodríguez, who said that Waltz was “blatantly lying” and that his “attitude is disgraceful.” He further stated: “Mr. Waltz is lying again, and I wish him a better future in other roles, but at the United Nations and on the Security Council, his performance leaves much to be desired … He is undermining the dignity of the Cuban people and the Cuban government.”

articles.title: Thousands of farmers march for land rights in India’s Maharashtra
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Earlier this week, thousands of farmers in India’s western state of Maharashtra marched to its capital, Mumbai, and forced the state government to recognize their right to the land they have tilled for years and fulfill their demands. Over 12,000 in number, the farmers, carrying red flags and shouting slogans against the ultra-right-wing government led by the Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), were led by the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS), a left-wing farmers’ union. The farmers were also supported by several other left-wing mass organizations, such as the Center for Indian Trade Unions (CITU) and Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI). The farmers started their march on foot and in hundreds of vehicles from Akole on Monday and were aiming to reach the residence of the state’s Chief Minister in Mumbai, a distance of around 200 km, where they were about to organize an indefinite sit-in to press for their demands. The major demands of the farmers were recognition of their rights over the lands they have been tilling for generations, adequate compensation for crops lost due to this years’ drought and a loan waiver of at least Rs 200,000 (around 2,100 USD) among others. The call for the march to Mumbai came after the government failed to respond to the farmers’ demand during a six-day sit-in between October 21 to 26 in Akole. Before starting to march to Mumbai the farmers also carried out a march in Akole itself. The government initially failed to respond to the farmers’ demand and instead threatened them with police action and sent notices asking them to end the agitation. AIKS responded by saying in its press release on Monday that “people’s problems cannot be made to disappear by issuing notices or resorting to pressure” and announced the march to Mumbai. The farmers marched for two days before the government called for negotiations on Tuesday and later announced an agreement on all major demands. Land rights and drought relief A large number of farmers in Maharashtra and other regions of the country cultivate the land without having any documentary proof of their ownership. The governments often recognize such lands as forest areas or put them under categories which makes it impossible to claim private ownership. This often creates threats of eviction and the deprivation of the only source of livelihoods for millions of peasants. AIKS in Maharashtra has been demanding recognition of the ownership of the peasants on the land they have tilled for generations and has led various successful movements for the same in different parts of the state in the past decade. Earlier this year it led a similar movement in the state’s Nashik district, forcing the government to acknowledge the issue and promise reforms. In addition to the long-term problem of ownership, several of the states in India faced a deficient monsoon this year, affecting agriculture adversely and creating losses to millions of farmers in the country. In Maharashtra alone, the government has declared 265 out of 358 administrative units ( Taluks ) as “drought affected.” Most of the state governments have failed to provide any meaningful relief to the farmers yet. However, under pressure, the Maharashtra government recently announced a Rs 5,000 (around 50 USD) compensation for each farming family in the drought-affected regions, inviting strong reactions from the farmers over the paltry amount. AIKS called the government’s announcement of the drought relief “grossly inadequate” and a “cruel mockery of the losses suffered by the peasantry.” It demanded that compensation must be based on the actual losses faced by the peasants, including a waiver from paying the loans up to Rs 200,000.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s stalemate and the liberal fantasy of a new Israel
articles.author: Abdaljawad Omar
articles.content: Liberal commentary frames Israel’s elections as a struggle for its soul, but the opposition offers only better management of the same system. Record Palestinian turnout reflects hope for modest relief, not real change.

articles.title: No seat at the table: Israel’s post-election message to its Palestinian citizens
articles.author: Qassam Muaddi
articles.content: Netanyahu's party and the Israeli opposition are at an electoral stalemate that only an alliance with the Palestinian citizens of Israel can break, but neither camp is willing to extend their democratic ideals to the Arab lists who won 19 seats in the latest election.

articles.title: Meet AI Engineer Who Resigned from DeepMind over “Google’s Complicity in the Gaza Genocide”
articles.content: Several tech workers at Google’s AI unit DeepMind have resigned in protest over the tech giant’s work with the U.S. and Israeli militaries. Last week, DeepMind research engineer Sofia Liguori announced her resignation in a letter to her colleagues titled “Stay Human.” She denounced what she called “Google’s complicity in the Gaza genocide” and the increasing integration of Google’s technology into military and surveillance systems. “I felt I could not, in good faith, send this message of building AI to benefit humanity while ignoring that our company was complicit in a genocide,” Liguori tells Democracy Now! “The problem is that when the focus is on the model capabilities and on the potential for agents 'going rogue,' we are shifting the attention from a specific human choice … which is this unrestrained, unregulated integration of the systems without red lines.”

articles.title: Israeli Elections to Global Movements: Tariq Ali, Rashid Khalidi on New Book “The Neck and the Sword”
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. ANJALI KAMAT : Israel is facing possible political gridlock after neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his chief challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, won enough seats to form a new government in Tuesday’s election. The final tally could take days. The election marked the first time Israelis went to the polls since the October 7th, 2023, attack and the ensuing wars on Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The vote drew record turnout. With over 70% of the vote counted, Israeli — Netanyahu’s Likud party leads with the 27 seats, ahead of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party at 22. According to Haaretz , a possible pro-Netanyahu coalition currently has 54 seats, while a possible pro-Eisenkot bloc has 49 seats. Palestinian-led parties — the Joint list and Ra’am — have won 17 seats, their strongest showing ever. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out governing with the Arab parties. Millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are ineligible to vote. This is Netanyahu speaking on Tuesday. PRIME MINISTER BENJAMIN NETANYAHU : [translated] We must form a right-wing, national, strong government. That is what must be done. We must not — must not — endanger Israel and establish a government that is backed by anti-Zionist Arab parties. … Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner, President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. AMY GOODMAN : Meanwhile, former General Gadi Eisenkot said the election results are a vote against the continued leadership of Netanyahu. GADI EISENKOT : [translated] I stand before you thrilled. This morning, the people of Israel went to a referendum on the leadership that will guide Israel in the coming years. Tonight, we received an answer. The public has decided in favor of change. AMY GOODMAN : Eisenkot also accused Netanyahu of using Israel’s security for his political needs. And this is Yousef Jabareen, Palestinian citizen of Israel and head of the Joint List, speaking Tuesday. YOUSEF JABAREEN : [translated] We are the people who sent Ben-Gvir home. It’s us, our people, our nation. … The exit polls indicate that we have achieved our goal. The Joint List is a strong force that will bring change and make a difference. AMY GOODMAN : For more about the election, Palestine and beyond, we’re joined in studio by two guests. They’ve just co-authored a new book. It’s titled The Neck and the Sword: Palestine’s Unfinished Struggle . Rashid Khalidi is a Palestinian American historian and Edward Said professor emeritus of modern Arab studies at Columbia University. His books include The Hundred Years’ War on Palestine . And Tariq Ali is a Pakistani British historian, activist, filmmaker and longtime associate of the New Left Review . His books include You Can’t Please All: Memoirs 1980-2024 . We welcome you both back to Democracy Now! Rashid Khalidi, let’s begin with you. The results are not final right now in Israel, but it does look like Netanyahu has pulled ahead, and it looks like the Joint List has garnered more votes than they ever have in history. Can you talk about the significance of these elections and what it means for either of the men to become prime minister? RASHID KHALIDI : Well, the so-called Arab parties, the Palestinian parties, have done better than they ever did before. The problem is that the rest of the parties in the Israeli political spectrum refuse to govern with Arabs. This is — there’s a deeply seated racism. You heard Netanyahu talking about we’ve — “we’re going to deal with the danger of these Arab parties, these anti-Zionist Arab parties.” So, neither party, neither coalition has won. There’s a very good question as to what difference there is between the two coalitions when you’re talking about anything that deals with Arabs, Palestinians, Israel’s aggression throughout the region. Both seem committed to continuation of the war on Gaza. Both seem committed to hostility to Iran. And neither coalition seems willing to change anything fundamental about Israel, except things that deal with, essentially, Jewish citizens. So, one group wants the judicial reform to stop; the other — that is to say, Netanyahu — wants to move towards authoritarianism. Well, that’s fine as far as Jewish citizens are concerned. But the discrimination against Arabs within Israel and Israel’s wars do not seem to be on the table for either of the two major coalitions, and they refuse to govern with the Arab parties, which actually hold the balance right now. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Rashid and Tariq, you both talk quite a bit about how the genocide in Gaza has dramatically changed public opinion in this country, particularly among young people. You also acknowledge there can be quite a gap between that change in public opinion — RASHID KHALIDI : Right. ANJALI KAMAT : — translating to an actual change in the material conditions on the grounds for Palestinians in particular. We’ve got the midterms coming up next week. It’s the middle of this unpopular war in Iran, soaring gas prices, inflation. And we’re also seeing resistance to AIPAC — RASHID KHALIDI : Right. ANJALI KAMAT : — in many of the campaigns. Are you hopeful that the results of this election, or even just this campaign, might help shift U.S. policy towards Israel? RASHID KHALIDI : Well, public opinion has shifted. The people have voted with their feet, as it were, against not just AIPAC , but against this war. Everybody’s against this war — right, left, center. It’s very, very clear that the suffering in terms of gas prices and inflation, and so on and so forth, is a direct result of Trump’s stupid war on Iran. The question is: Will people be able to overcome the resistance of the elites in this country, which seem still totally committed to support of Israel? And that actually is most true of the Republican Party, but it’s true also of the Democratic Party. So, the question is: Will the voters on Tuesday be able to force the parties, especially the Democratic Party, to actually do something to change American policy, stop arms to Israel, force the president to stop his war? That’s not going to be a — that’s going to be a tall order. So, public opinion has shifted. The politicians, the elites, not so much. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Tariq Ali, I want to bring you into the conversation. Your read on the midterms coming up, and also the results of the Israeli elections? TARIQ ALI : Well, the result of the Israeli elections, I concur totally with what Rashid has said. Quite honestly, it’s not going to make any difference for the, you know, Palestinian population inside Israel. And what is quite staggering is this decision to treat the Palestinians, the Arab Palestinians of Israel, as an invisible people carries on. You know, they’ve just won 17 seats, their largest number in the Knesset, and they’re being told, “You don’t really exist. We just pretend that you exist for international reasons. Ideally, we’d quite like to wipe you out, but let’s start by wiping you out politically.” That is the only reason why they’re not treated as a political party and allowed to function and make coalitions with whoever they want to. Were they allowed to do so, well, Netanyahu would be out of power, because whatever the similarities between the two coalitions, I think a defeat for — Netanyahu’s removal, on its own, would mean something, saying that the archcriminal, wanted by the International Criminal Court, has at least been removed from office. It looks as if even that might — it might not happen. The effect on the midterms, we shall see. I mean, you know, the Democrats have been incredibly slow, to put it at its mildest, in realizing that the bulk of the country is opposed to them on this question. And the victory of Mamdani in New York and the winning of primary seats by DSA candidates is an indication of public opinion — a small indication, but an important one. So, if we have a few Senate seats in Michigan or from Florida, which would be a miracle, going to the DSA Democrats, then, you know, some change is on the way. The monolithic impression which one gets of Congress and Senate on key security issues would be pierced a tiny bit. The big question is: Are the Democrats going to win the Senate? That is what Trump is fighting for: “OK, let them have the House, but the Senate, we must keep.” But if they lose the majority in the Senate, it is a, you know, serious setback for MAGA and for that faction in American politics. AMY GOODMAN : Tariq Ali, you live in London. Rashid, you live here in New York. President Trump just put on social media — he refers to himself in the third person. He said, “When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu. It all took place AFTER the Endorsement by President Trump, who only wants what is good for the Middle East, Israel, and the United States of America!” But can you talk about, Rashid Khalidi, the role of the United States in these elections, but also in the course Israel is taking right now? RASHID KHALIDI : I mean, Israel for three years has been fighting a war side by side with the United States. Nothing that they do would be possible without the fact that every single combat aircraft is American; the 2,000-pound bombs are American; the vetoes in the Security Council, multiple vetoes preventing a ceasefire, were American. And one could go on. Tens of billions of dollars came from the United States to fund this war. So this was an American-Israeli war — or, if you prefer, Israeli-American war. That’s the American role. Israel has now occupied extraordinary amounts of extra territory, in Lebanon, in Syria and in the Gaza Strip, and is ravaging the West Bank. And that’s the Israeli government and its settlers and its army that are doing it. This is not a bunch of crazy settlers. This is the Israeli government, led by two of the most intensely right-wing ministers in Israeli history, which is saying a lot given Israeli history. So, a change in the United States will force a change in Israeli behavior. The question is, as Tariq said: Is it going to be a minor change, or is it going to be a big one? And I’m not enormously optimistic about this midterm. But public opinion is not going to shift back. People have seen something that cannot be unseen. They’ve seen genocide. They’ve seen slaughter. And Israel has no defense. You have to call people who say anything about Israel antisemitic, because you can’t answer 20,000 dead children. How do you speak to that? Burning olive groves, beating up journalists. You cannot justify anything Israel does, so you resort to the lowest of possible epithets, saying that someone is antisemitic, simply because they’re criticizing Israel. And that’s the situation that they’re in. They’re really in a corner. And were it not for Trump and were it not for American support, Israel would have lost. We can see Europe, even Europe, moving slowly toward sanctions. So, I think that that trajectory is clear. But the question is: How quickly? How much suffering will be inflicted by Israel and the United States in Lebanon, Syria, and especially in Gaza and the West Bank, before this monolithic offensive of these two powers — it is the United States and Israel; it’s not just Israel — is stopped? And I don’t see that coming out of our midterms, unfortunately. I hope — I hope there’ll be a change, but I don’t see — I don’t see this bulldozer stopped. ANJALI KAMAT : You know, speaking of Europe, Tariq, talk about — you know, we’ve seen this massive number of protests on the continent going on right now, about the cost of living, critiques of the government. But you’ve also had massive pro-Palestinian demonstrations across the continent and in the U.K., but you’ve also had a doubling down in some of these countries, particularly the U.K., France and Germany, on any sort of pro-Palestinian speech and action. Can you talk about the latest with what’s happening in the U.K. with the crackdown on Palestine Action? TARIQ ALI : Well, the crackdown on Palestine Action, which is a group of nonviolent peace activists determined to do their best to help the Palestinians in a more concrete way than simply marching on the streets, who’ve targeted Israeli arms factories and people collaborating with them in the United States — attempts to stop them failed, because juries acquitted them when they explained what they were doing. Then there was a big move: Let’s abolish juries. That’s the problem. The problem is not what Israel is doing, but what the juries are doing, acquitting activists. So, that didn’t work, either. There was a lot of anger about that. So, then, what to do? I’m told that what happened was that the Palestine Action people, to show their anger against Trump and American collaboration with the Israelis, damaged some tiny bit of Trump’s golf course in Scotland. And this, you know, very sort of trivial act, really, angered the great leader of the United States, and he demanded that they be dealt with, that this is how the question of even banning them arose. No Cabinet minister can explain this. The head of security in 10 Downing Street, Jonathan Powell, has made it clear he thinks this is a foolish measure. Jonathan Powell’s wife has supported Palestine Action. You know, this is the equivalent of the head of the FBI , or whatever, supporting something that is happening against the government. She said, “I visited Palestine 20 years ago as a journalist. I saw what they do on the West Bank. And Palestine Action has my support.” Were they going to now charge her for aiding terrorism? They drew back. So, once you draw back because an important person has said it, then your case falls. So, we’ll see what happens. AMY GOODMAN : In September, the British Labour Party held its annual conference in Liverpool. We were in London, and just as we were going to air, the British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband took the stage. This is an excerpt of what he said. ED MILIBAND : And I want to say to the millions of people in this country, and indeed elsewhere, who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: We hear you. You were right. … We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with action. We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government says: We will not let you succeed. AMY GOODMAN : So, that was British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband standing in front of a sign that said “Hope Again.” It got some of the largest applause we had seen. Interestingly, Ed Milliband, formerly an intern at The Nation magazine. But if you can talk, Tariq Ali, about the significance of what he said versus what U.K. is doing? TARIQ ALI : I think he meant it. His mother died recently, and she was a Palestinian activist. She had lost her — you know, large chunks of her family during the Judeocide of the Second World War. And she said, “I cannot bear to see what Israel is doing. They’re doing a version of what was done to us.” And she marched on every single demonstration with the Jewish bloc, which is part of the Palestinian solidarity movement. And Edward used to listen to her every day. And at at her funeral, which I attended, Edward said very openly, he said, “You know, sometimes I’d look at my mother, and she had her hands on her head like this and would say, 'Why, oh why?' And I would say, 'Mum, why are you saying, “Why, oh why?”' She’s saying, 'Why both my sons joined this wretched Labour Party?'” So, he said, “She had many 'Why, oh why?' moments, so I will never forget her stand on Palestine.” And it was very moving. But I think underneath it was also — because, obviously, it had been approved by the new leader — to win back Muslim votes. I think there was a cynical calculation there. I’m sure Edward believes all that he said, but it’s had nil impact. AMY GOODMAN : And by the way, Miliband’s speech came a day after police arrested more than 50 people outside the Labour Party conference, with demonstrators nonviolently urging that the banned direct action group Palestine Action be supported. Among them, Robert Del Naja, frontman for the British trip-hop group Massive Attack, arrested for holding some homemade banners reading “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” TARIQ ALI : You know, this campaign against Palestine Action, I have sort of referred to it as a campaign against elderly people, because they’ve arrested more old-age pensioners who’ve come out and demonstrated, of all nationalities, of all ethnicities, picked up, put in buses, one woman on wheelchair. I mean, the whole thing makes the British government a laughingstock. And if they were clever, they would just give a nod and a wink to the Supreme Court, which is listening to the case, and say, “OK, lose it.” They’re saying, “We’re waiting for the judges.” But that’s not true, because the previous judges acquitted them. Government took the case to the Supreme Court. They could easily withdraw the case, and that would be that. But that would be a huge defeat for what has become, stupidly, a central plank of their policy. So, there’s no basic difference between the new prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, in my opinion, very little difference at all on Palestine. They’ve made this slight move, but have done nothing. And we always judge people by what they do, not by what they say. ANJALI KAMAT : Let’s talk about the title of your new book, The Neck and the Sword . It’s a reference to a phrase used by the great Palestinian writer and journalist Ghassan Kanafani. He was a spokesperson for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the PFLP , and founding editor of its weekly magazine, Al-Hadaf . He also wrote some of the most iconic novels in Palestinian literature, including Men in the Sun and Returning to Haifa , among others. Ghassan Kanafani was assassinated by Israel in a 1972 car bombing. Two years before, he spoke to Richard Carleton from the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. They spoke in Beirut. Here’s a clip from that interview. RICHARD CARLETON : Why won’t your organization engage in peace talks with the Israelis? GHASSAN KANAFANI : You don’t mean exactly peace talks. You mean capitulation, surrendering. RICHARD CARLETON : Why not just talk? GHASSAN KANAFANI : Talk to whom? RICHARD CARLETON : Talk to the Israeli leaders. GHASSAN KANAFANI : That’s kind of conversation between the sword and the neck, you mean. RICHARD CARLETON : Well, if there were no swords and no guns in the room, you could still talk. GHASSAN KANAFANI : No. I haven’t been — I have never seen any talk between a colonialist case and a national liberation movement. RICHARD CARLETON : But despite this, why not talk? GHASSAN KANAFANI : Talk about what? RICHARD CARLETON : Talk about the possibility of not fighting. GHASSAN KANAFANI : Not fighting for what? RICHARD CARLETON : Not fighting at all, no matter what for. GHASSAN KANAFANI : Ya’ni , people usually fight for something, and they stop fighting for something. So, you can’t tell me even why should we speak about what. RICHARD CARLETON : Well, stop fighting. GHASSAN KANAFANI : Fight for what, or talk about stop fighting — why? RICHARD CARLETON : Talk to stop fighting to stop the death and the misery, the destruction, the pain. GHASSAN KANAFANI : The misery and the destruction and the pain and the death of whom? RICHARD CARLETON : Of Palestinians, of Israelis, of Arabs. GHASSAN KANAFANI : Of the Palestinian people who are uprooted, thrown in the camps, living in starvation, killed for 20 years and forbidden to use even the name Palestinians. RICHARD CARLETON : They’re better that way than dead, though. GHASSAN KANAFANI : Maybe to you. But to us, it’s not. To us, to liberate our country, to have dignity, to have respect, to have our mere human rights, is something as essential as life itself. ANJALI KAMAT : Ghassan Kanafani talking to Richard Carleton from the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in 1970. Rashid Khalidi, why did you decide to call this set of conversations between you and Tariq Ali The Neck and the Sword ? RASHID KHALIDI : Well, many reasons. First of all, it was a reference to this wonderful, charismatic and extraordinarily intelligent Palestinian intellectual, murdered simply because his words were too dangerous for Israel to tolerate. AMY GOODMAN : And how was he murdered? RASHID KHALIDI : He was blown up with his 17-year-old niece in his car as he was about to drive her away from his home in 1972. And it was — it has been intolerable for Israel that people like him or Kamal Nasser or many, many, many other Palestinian writers and intellectuals make a case that Israel basically cannot answer, so they kill them. I mean, the number of Palestinian leaders and intellectuals who’ve been assassinated by Israel is extraordinarily long. The other reason was that he and I, Tariq and I, had done several sessions, one of which was previously published, of conversations, in which we went over this genocidal war and we talked about deeper roots than just, you know, what started on the 7th of October. One of the worst things about the way in which this has been treated is as if history started on the 7th of October. Well, we have the Nakba in 1948. We have things — in fact, we started talking about the '30s and Britain destroying Palestinian society in order to help the creation of and establishment of Israel. That's the beginning of, in fact, our discussion. ANJALI KAMAT : And the colonial techniques and the training they gave the Israelis. RASHID KHALIDI : Exactly. We went into the fact that everything the Israeli army does, its attacks on civilians, are a result of British counterinsurgency doctrine, that was passed on to the Israeli army by the British during the 1930s. So, we went deeper than not just October 7th, before October 7th. And somehow, Ghassan was central to much of what we talked about. Verso and the Institute for Palestine Studies has also published a book by Ghassan Kanafani. ANJALI KAMAT : And you have an introduction to that. RASHID KHALIDI : To which I wrote — ANJALI KAMAT : And you talk about the different forms of resistance. RASHID KHALIDI : Right. ANJALI KAMAT : What is your sense of the state of Palestinian resistance today? I mean, we’re into the fourth year of this ongoing genocide. RASHID KHALIDI : Right. ANJALI KAMAT : The U.N. commission of inquiry just said that what’s happening in the West Bank is also crimes against humanity. RASHID KHALIDI : Well, I think that the most effective forms of resistance right now, in many cases, are the kinds of things that people are doing in the U.K., Palestine Action, BDS . This upheaval on American campuses, I think, woke American — the American public up. That was not Palestinian resistance, but that was inspired by the fact that the Palestinians are still standing tall in spite of everything Israel has done to them. People saw that genocide, and they were moved, especially young people. But that’s affected American public opinion and global public opinion. AMY GOODMAN : I mean, Zohran Mamdani has become mayor. And what did he campaign on? Gasoline prices and Gaza. RASHID KHALIDI : Exactly. AMY GOODMAN : And you were a professor at Columbia, now professor emeritus, with his father, Mahmood Mamdani — RASHID KHALIDI : Right. AMY GOODMAN : — also a very powerful voice on the issue of Palestine. RASHID KHALIDI : I mean, they are trying to silence these voices, student voices. The repression on campus is extraordinary. And I don’t just talk about Columbia. Every single American campus, the elites that control these campuses will not allow criticism of Israel. The things that have been done to pro-Palestine demonstrators on American campuses were never done in the anti-apartheid movement, in the movement for climate change, in the movement even against the Vietnam War. I’m going back to my youth, my student days. Nothing like what has been done on American campuses was done to students, because they are terrified at the fact that the students have a case. What Israel is doing is abominable, and people are increasingly understanding that. So you shut it down. And I think that there is resistance simply on the ground. People staying in their homes are, in fact, resisting. That’s another enormously important form of resistance. But in international law, resistance, armed resistance and multiple other forms, are legal. What Kanafani was saying in this book is writing, culture, literature are enormously important forms of resistance. And he was talking about specific writers — Mahmoud Darwish, Tawfiq Ziad and so on. And he was the first to talk about them. This is a book published in 1968. And I think that that’s true to this day. I think that what people are saying, what people are writing, the books that are being published today are an enormously important form of resistance. AMY GOODMAN : We’re going to break, and we also want to talk about Iran and much more with Rashid Khalidi and Tariq Ali, co-authors of the new book The Neck and the Sword: Palestine’s Unfinished Struggle . We’ll return to them after a short break. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Sonny Singh in our Democracy Now! studio. This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. ANJALI KAMAT : We’re speaking to Rashid Khalidi and Tariq Ali, co-authors of the new book The Neck and the Sword: Palestine’s Unfinished Struggle . Let’s talk about the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Iran’s response, and how that’s changing the balance of forces in the region. We’re seeing a flurry of reports that the U.S. and Israel are drawing up plans to attack Iran after the midterms. Meanwhile, a Reuters investigation this month found that Iran created far more damage in the Gulf than the Gulf states had previously admitted. And you’ve got Ansar Allah in Yemen also blocking shipping routes, attacking strategic sites in Saudi Arabia. And you have the so-called Mecca Defense Alliance, which is Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, who were all in Iran this week. And now Egypt has agreed to provide military support for Saudi Arabia in its fight against Ansar Allah. And Drop Site News reports that the UAE is backing Ansar Allah in Yemen. What is the regional picture, Tariq Ali, and why do you think the Trump administration keeps trying to fight what many are calling an unwinnable war with Iran? TARIQ ALI : Well, I think the Trump administration made a huge mistake, and some of the people within the administration are aware of it, as is virtually the entire American military elite. It was a disaster for them to do this. There was debate before, and Trump overrode them under pressure from the war criminal Netanyahu. That is effectively what took place, and now they are paying the price. They thought Iran would crumble. Trump said it’d be — “We thought it’d be like Venezuela. We’d have our own person in there.” Well, it wasn’t like that. They misjudged Iran. They misjudged the support for Palestine and for Iranian national sovereignty. And then, the Iranians did something that took the world by surprise: They hit back. You’re not meant to hit back when the world’s largest imperial power is attacking you. You’re meant to sit still and do nothing. Well, the Iranians did what any self-respecting nation would do: They hit back. And when they hit back, they targeted first all the U.S. bases in the region. They virtually destroyed the naval base in Bahrain. They attacked bases in Kuwait. They bombed the Gulf states, unheard of. And I’m told — I was told by friends, Palestinian friends in Jordan, that many Jordanians came out onto the streets as they saw these missiles and drones flying, and said, “Please don’t forget us. A few bombs here would help, too, get rid of the monarchy.” So, effectively, the Iranians transformed the situation. And that is why the crisis is now exacerbated. And there’s very little they can do except do a deal. So, you ask about the Ansar Allah, the Yemeni nationalists, attacking Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has occupied them for years, with the support of the West, imposed a corrupt puppet government on them, which they are now getting rid of systematically, from town after town after town. And then they’ve attacked Saudi Arabia itself. So, Saudi Arabia has money, so they’re offering Pakistan and Turkey $8 billion each. The Egyptians are greedier, because the Americans have spoiled them, so their army will probably demand more than $8 billion. The Egyptians should be wary, because even their most gifted leader tried the intervention in Yemen under — you know, during Gamal Abdel Nasser’s reign, to attack people who were pro-imperialist, but they suffered. There is this instinct in the Yemenis: They don’t like being occupied. It’s quite nice to have one country where its people feel that, you know, occupation is a debased thing. So they are fighting back. This is what’s created the crisis. And I think the Americans are buying time by using the Mecca Three in order to delay the process. Pakistan, Turkey will not — and leave alone Saudi Arabia — will not do anything against the will of the United States, in my opinion. They’ve never done so. AMY GOODMAN : This is Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi last week during the Egypt Forum 2026 in Cairo, saying that Egypt will provide military support for Saudi Arabia as the Ansar Allah movement, the Houthis, continue to strike crucial refinery infrastructure within the kingdom. PRESIDENT ABDEL FATTAH EL- SISI : [translated] Standing with our brothers in the Gulf is an extension of the mutual Arab national security between us and all our efforts. And by the way, so people can understand, because I have heard a lot of talk over the past few days saying that we are going to launch an attack on Yemen and things of that nature, absolutely not. We have never cooperated to fight beyond the borders. We are talking about defending the kingdom’s territory and its borders, defending the lands of the kingdom’s and its borders, the lands of any other Arab country and its borders, if we have been asked to do so by the country itself. But we do not extend our military efforts beyond the borders of Egypt or any other brotherly country who care about its security and stability. AMY GOODMAN : So, that is the Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. I’m wondering if you can address this, Rashid Khalidi, and also now knowing that the UAE is supporting the Houthis and this different alignments of power. RASHID KHALIDI : Well, just starting from what Tariq said, the Iranians have shown themselves to be enormously resilient. They have closed the Straits of Hormuz. Their allies in Yemen are basically winning a civil war and fighting off Saudi Arabia. Countries in the region, including countries that are completely aligned with the United States, are beginning to wonder, “Who can protect us — not just from Iran, but also from Israel?” Remember, Israel attacked Qatar. Israel has attacked, in addition to invading south Lebanon, has attacked Syria. And it is something that has changed the face of this entire region. The United States’ mistaken, foolish attack on Iran has unleashed forces that were totally contained previously, or seemed to be contained. And I think that you have governments that are, as Tariq exactly said, aligned completely with Washington, wondering, “Will these people protect us? Do they care about anybody in this region besides Israel?” And the answer is obviously no and no. And so, the United Arab Emirates, which has been at odds with Saudi Arabia for many years, and that’s come to a head recently, are now playing an extraordinarily dubious, dangerous game, not just in Yemen. They are the main supporters of the Rapid Support Forces, so-called, in Sudan, carrying on a war that is genocidal in nature. They are the supporters of one faction in Libya. They are involved in the Horn of Africa in ways that actually counter the interests of other regional powers. So I think everything has been turned upside down in a way. ANJALI KAMAT : And the UAE is a close ally of Israel, as well. TARIQ ALI : Yes. RASHID KHALIDI : It is the closest ally of Israel. It is the only real ally of Israel in the region. So, you have some very strange things happening as a result, essentially, of the American-Israeli decision to attack Iran. They have unleashed a hornet’s nest, if you want. And it’s not — you cannot put that genie back in the bottle. The world oil prices are not going to go back down very soon. The fears that have been aroused in Gulf countries about the vulnerability of their desalination plants, of their oil refineries, of their entire infrastructure, to $25,000 drones fired only 20 or 30 miles across the Gulf, those fears are not going to go away. The vulnerability of those countries is now laid bare, and the idiocy of American bases being placed in proximity to Iran, that have been, as Tariq said, systematically destroyed. The entire logistical base of the U.S. Navy in Bahrain was destroyed. The logistical base of the American Air Force and Army in Kuwait and in other parts of the Gulf was destroyed in a matter of a few days by the Iranians, with cheap weapons, leading the United States to use up huge stocks of enormously expensive weapons, which actually were not able to stop the Iranians. So, regional balances have been changed. And what the UAE is doing here or what Egypt may do there is a function of, I think, their having lost a sense of how to deal with Iran and with Israel. They’re as scared, I think, now of Israel as they are of Iran. It has shown itself to be uncontrollable. And — AMY GOODMAN : So, I’m just wondering, as we begin to wrap up this show — Tariq Ali, we’re in this moment of rising fascism in the world, but you also have these youth-led movements across Europe and India. And now we see what’s happened in Brazil with the reelection of President Lula, and Bolsonaro, his opponent, the son of the previous president, who’s now under house arrest for a failed coup attempt in Brazil — Flávio Bolsonaro flees to the United States with his family. If you can talk about your hope for the future? TARIQ ALI : Well, it’s a bit difficult to talk about hope in these awful conditions. The movements are, of course, great. But even in the case of Lula’s triumph, which is fantastic — and, you know, I’m delighted and thrilled — but the PT, as a political party, was smashed in the Brazilian elections, which means it will be very difficult for Lula to do too much. That’s the problem. Even the student movement, which has won in Serbia, as it did in Nepal a few years ago — AMY GOODMAN : Knocked out Vučić. TARIQ ALI : Yeah. They change — they form a government, then they don’t know what to do, because neoliberalism has gone so deep that there are problems. We’ll see what happens in France, where there is a real danger that someone whose party is linearly of fascist descent, in Marine Le Pen, will probably be backed by liberals to defeat the left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. If you look at how they are normalizing in the Financial Times and The Economist , it’s quite frightening. So, they’re going for the far right, feeling these are the only people who can deal with protests. But the interesting thing about these protests also is, whereas in the ’60s and ’70s Vietnam triggered these mega-protests, including in the U.S., today the anti-imperial issue is Palestine. Even in countries with no history of a Palestine solidarity movement, suddenly the Palestine flag emerges. Why? Because their governments are trying to stop dissent on this issue, so they are defying their governments. And in Albania, when the students and others found out that the Supreme Court had decided to not accept — AMY GOODMAN : We have 10 seconds. TARIQ ALI : — the removal of Kushner, they burned the Supreme Court down. So, that’s a sort of strange situation we’re in. There’s absolutely no confidence in the ruling elites, so people are, you know, burning down buildings. I mean, Albania was a total puppet state of the United States after the collapse of communism. This is what’s happening there now. So, it’s a deep crisis. How it will be resolved, we shall see. AMY GOODMAN : Well, we’re going to leave it there for now, Tariq Ali and Rashid Khalidi, co-authors of the new book The Neck and the Sword: Palestine’s Unfinished Struggle . Thank you so much for joining us. That does it for today’s show. Coming up tomorrow, we’ll speak to a research engineer for Google’s AI unit DeepMind, who’s just resigned over Google’s work with the U.S. and Israeli militaries. And tune in on election night, Tuesday, November 3rd, for Democracy Now! 's four-hour live election night special starting 8 p.m. Eastern. That's Tuesday, November 3rd. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. Thanks.

articles.title: ICE arrests of Dominicans in Puerto Rico spark outrage and reignite calls for independence
articles.author: Devin B. Martinez
articles.content: Masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents carrying long guns swept through working-class neighborhoods in San Juan, Puerto Rico between October 22-25. About a dozen workers, largely Dominican immigrants, were reportedly detained from Río Piedras, Capetillo, Villa Palmeras, Villa Capri, and Barrio Obrero. Local leaders and community members have expressed outrage over the ICE deployment to the island. Protests have also broken out, demanding ICE out of Puerto Rico and elevating calls for independence from the United States. During the operations, federal agents claimed that they were detaining criminals, but locals say they were all hard working people, many with families. Elected officials speak out against ICE deployment The Dominican Republic sits about 50 miles from Puerto Rico. Dating back to the pre-Colombian era, the Caribbean has always been closely linked by migration and maritime mobility. There has never been a time where the islands existed in isolation. That might help explain why immigration arrests and deportations are being met with such deep rejection. Puerto Rico’s Senate opposition spokesman, Luis Javier Hernández Ortiz and the mayor of San Juan, Miguel Romero have all condemned the ICE raids. Romero ordered the municipal police to not assist federal agents with any ICE operations. The island’s American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) branch also condemned the raids and characterized the operations as a pattern of violence and intimidation. “We strongly reject the massive deployment of ICE agents who, in a threatening manner and armed with long guns, continue occupying the streets,” said Annette Martínez Orabona, executive director of the ACLU of PR, in a statement. ICE had no judicial warrant for anyone they arrested, said the legal director of ACLU of PR, Fermín L. Arraiza-Havas, speaking to El Grito Media . Local officials blame the island government’s alleged “voluntary handover” of data for making the sweeping operations possible. Puerto Rican government collaborates with ICE The ACLU of PR says the Puerto Rican government gave ICE the personal information of thousands of immigrant drivers, in violation of a 2013 confidentiality law. The information was handed over by Transportation Secretary Edwin González and Governor of Puerto Rico Jenniffer González-Colón. “The laws in Puerto Rico protected that information,” said ACLU’s Arraiza-Havas to El Grito Media. In a statement provided to The San Juan Daily Star , ACLU’s Martínez Orabona accused the governor of facilitating the federal immigration raids by “providing residential addresses and confidential information belonging to more than 6,000 immigrants residing in Puerto Rico.” “Both the federal and state governments are responsible for the escalation of violence that we are seeing from ICE,” Martínez Orabona said. The ACLU of PR held a press conference on October 15, where they made public the mass data sharing between the Puerto Rican government and ICE. Border czar Tom Homan then visited Puerto Rico on Oct 21-22 to review immigration enforcement efforts and operational challenges, according to The Washington Post . ICE raids began the next day. Locals confront federal agents as raids sweep Dominican neighborhoods Various videos have circulated online, where community members can be seen surrounding ICE vehicles and confronting agents , most of whom spoke English, as they arrested individuals. One restaurant worker reportedly refused to let agents enter as they tried to follow a man they claimed was a criminal. The agents eventually left. ICE agents can also be seen in various videos threatening community defenders with pepper spray and tasers for legally recording their operations, as community members yell “Don’t touch me!” and “They’re taking hard working people from here, what a shame!” In at least one account, a Puerto Rican citizen (all Puerto Ricans are US citizens by birth) was stopped by a group of ICE agents who demanded his ID. The arrests have raised questions about racial profiling, citizen’s rights, as well as questions about the political direction of Puerto Rico. Colonialism or independence? Protests broke out in the neighborhoods targeted by ICE on Monday, October 26. The Fire Ants of Rio Piedras led a march, holding a banner that read “Heat for ICE Not for My Community” and “ICE Out!” Large groups of children and youth participated in the march. In a statement, the Feminist Collective PR, also part of the protests, said, “We reject this pathetic, collaborationist government that loves to bend its knees to Washington in exchange for nothing.” They argued that the same government that collaborates with the feds to hand over their Caribbean brothers and working people is also selling off the country piece by piece to foreigners coming to displace the Puerto Rican people. The group asserted that the foreigners that need to be removed are not Dominicans, but people like the Reuben Brothers – two British billionaires developing a multi-billion dollar resort and residential megaproject on the southwest coast. “The US has no moral integrity to stand on to come tell us here who can be our neighbors and who can’t.” Mounting resistance has also brought the call for Puerto Rican independence back into the spotlight. “ICE raids in Puerto Rico are colonial terrorism,” said Boricuas Unidos en la Diáspora, in a statement released on X. The group declared that ICE activity is part of the colonial status quo. The only two political options from here are: statehood, which they argue would only strengthen and perpetuate US federal control over Puerto Rico, and independence. “If you don’t want ICE roaming the streets of Puerto Rico, you have to support our nation’s independence,” the group said. “It’s that simple.”

articles.title: How did Lula win the election?
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: On October 25, Brazil’s three-time and current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, surprised the entire world by overcoming an electoral setback in the first round (in which he was defeated by the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro) and securing victory and the presidential seat in Brasília. Lula, the legendary union leader during the dictatorship, secured 51.79%, equivalent to 64,256,232 votes, while Bolsonaro (son of the detained former president Jair Bolsonaro) received 48.21%, or 59,826,041 votes. What is truly surprising about Bolsonaro’s defeat (given that most pollsters had predicted a very likely victory for him) is the enormous number of votes Lula managed to gain during the three weeks between the first and second rounds of voting. In that first round , Bolsonaro took first place with 48.21% (more than 56 million votes), and Lula came in second with 45.15% (just under 54 million votes). Many believed that the nearly 9 million votes obtained by all the other candidates combined in the first round would be distributed in a way more favorable to Bolsonaro, since most of those votes were cast for right-wing and center-right candidates. This seemed even more evident after many of the leaders of those parties endorsed Bolsonaro. Added to this question was the high probability that, in a society highly polarized between the two candidates, many voters who either cast blank or invalid ballots or abstained from voting in the first round would support one of the two candidates. Indeed, both of these circumstances played out. According to available data, more than 14 million Brazilians who had voted for other candidates, cast invalid ballots, or abstained from voting participated in the runoff, supporting either Lula or Bolsonaro. And this is precisely the key factor in understanding Lula’s victory. Assuming that very few voters would have switched their support from Lula to Bolsonaro or vice versa, it is important to note that of those 14 million votes that were redistributed, Lula managed to secure 10.37 million more votes than he received in the first round, while Bolsonaro managed to gain just under 4 million votes. This was enough for Lula not only to close the gap against his opponent but also to surpass him by a comfortable margin. What happened in Brazil? Faced with this surprising turn of events, hundreds of analysts in Latin America and around the world have rushed to present countless charts, hypotheses, and analyses in an effort to fully understand the reasons behind this victory. And the reasons have to do not only with the clearly impressive comeback by Lula’s Workers’ Party and its allies, but also with the fact that he appears to have put a halt to a seemingly unstoppable string of victories by the far right in Latin America. Given this, the question seems clear: How did Lula manage to convince such a staggering number of people to vote for him in the runoff who had not done so in the first round? In response, technical reasons have been put forward (such as campaign strategy, the use of social media, and mass mobilization), as well as political ones (fear of a far-right government, social-class alliances, the formation of a broad-based coalition, etc.). Among the technical reasons, Lula’s tremendous effort to turn the runoff campaign into a genuine, nearly constant mass mobilization (in both large cities and small towns) has been highlighted. The former union leader once again demonstrated his great charisma and ability to rally people before thousands of PT activists and members of other allied parties who fought day and night without stopping to overturn the result. Added to this is the PT’s digital strategy ; the party had repeatedly accused major social media platforms of boycotting the presidential campaign by hindering or reducing the visibility of Lula’s ads – but not those of Bolsonaro. In response, André Janones proposed a change in strategy. Lula’s WhatsApp channel grew from 3.7 million subscribers to more than 10 million in the span of 12 days. Through this channel, users were instructed to post certain messages, search for information online, comment on specific posts, and so on. In other words, to circumvent an algorithmic system that, they claimed, was deliberately sabotaging Lula’s campaign. The result was astonishing: despite the alleged media blockade on social media, the platforms were flooded with messages, images, and videos (many generated by AI) featuring Lula and attacking Bolsonaro’s candidacy, which undoubtedly had a major impact on the political communication strategy of the PT’s campaign, led by re-elected Governor Rafael Fonteles. For example, online interactions about Lula increased from 41% to 65% during the runoff election. But Lula also took the risk of bringing about tangible changes in people’s lives, and he sent what may have been his final message during the runoff election, when his party and allies succeeded in passing legislation to end the six-day workweek. The move was celebrated by the country’s workers and clearly gave Lula’s campaign a pro-worker tone. That is why he gained so many millions of votes in the second round of the election in the working-class suburbs of major cities. Read more: Brazil’s Congress ends 6×1 work schedule And yet, there remains a certain suspicion that if this set of measures had been applied in any other similar situation, something would have been missing to set it in motion and give deeper meaning to the purely political campaign – with its communication, marketing, and other tactical decisions. And that something is Lula. At times it seems that only someone with his political stature, his charisma, and the historic place he has already carved out in the history books could have won an election in Latin America against the far right, which enjoys the support of the most influential imperial powers of our time and an international oligarchy. The “warrior of the Brazilian people Lula achieved this, as already mentioned, thanks to a series of changes in his campaign strategy and concrete improvements in people’s lives. But it must be said without fear of contradiction: he did so by blending two dimensions that might seem contradictory, yet which a figure like him could bring together. The first is that, as some of his campaign strategists recount , he began to speak extensively about Brazil’s future despite having already served as president three times. In this way, he moved away from nostalgia for the past and began to speak of hope for the future. And second, Lula insisted throughout the campaign that this future was threatened by the Bolsonaros, whom he constantly linked to a submissive attitude toward US interests. In this way, Lula also employed a discourse of fear and danger, personifying it in Bolsonaro, who, as is well known, had reportedly left Brazil for the United States. But Lula did not do so in a pitiful or apocalyptic way; rather, he presented himself as the only one capable of halting that advance. And more than just capable, as the only one who, without a doubt, would do so. In other words, Lula established himself, at the age of 80, as a “warrior of the Brazilian people,” just as his supporters chanted in the streets. Then, in the debates (which undoubtedly had a huge impact on the runoff election) it seems Lula had had enough of the far right always appearing to be on the offensive, while the left and progressives always seemed to be waiting for the next blow. Lula put on his boxing gloves and began playing the game the far right had set for him … and won by knockout. And for that very reason, Lula, his followers, and many of those who supported him (not necessarily because they believe in his agenda, but because they feared a new far-right government, as the numbers show) must realize that, with a hostile legislature and an opposition united around a single family, Lula’s fourth term will likely be the most difficult of his life. Lula will have to seek ways to overcome the clear obstacles that the right and the far right will place in his path in order to achieve what he called “the best government in Brazil’s history.” For now, he has managed to prevent another Bolsonaro from reaching the presidency, but that does not mean the remainder of his term will be a “Brazilian pax.” In this regard, there is a Japanese proverb that Lula should keep in mind: “When you’ve won a battle, tighten your helmet.”

articles.title: Israel’s elections: all roads lead to genocide
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Israelis headed to voting centers on Tuesday, October 27, in legislative elections to choose the members of the parliament, known as the Knesset. The event marks Israel’s first general election since the October 7 attacks, which Netanyahu’s government expanded into a multi-front regional war. Who is competing in the elections? For many, these elections serve as a direct referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the far-right bloc he heads. The Pro-Netanyahu Bloc This bloc comprises the National Liberal Party ( Likud ) led by Netanyahu, the Religious Zionist Party ( HaTzionut HaDatit ) led by current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, and Jewish Power Party ( Otzma Yehudit ) led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. The coalition advocates for the consolidation of Israeli rule throughout the occupied Palestinian territories, explicitly rejects the possibility of Palestinian statehood, promotes the expansion of settlements and the implementation of hardline security measures against Palestinians. It also calls for disavowing the Oslo Accords, and the total disarmament of Hamas. The anti-Netanyahu bloc The primary competitor to Netanyahu and his coalition is the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief of the Israeli forces. It represents a center-right to center-left opposition when it comes to Israeli internal affairs, but of course not to Palestinians and their destiny. Eisenkot is the architect of the “Dahiya Doctrine,” an Israeli military strategy that calls for applying massive, disproportionate firepower and the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure in order to create long-term deterrence, and discourage the local population from supporting any force resisting Israel. He was also a member of Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Eisenkot’s bloc includes the Yashar Party, led by Eisenkot, and the Together alliance ( Beyachad ), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett. It also includes The Democrats (HaDemokratim) – a merger of the Labor and Meretz parties – led by Yair Golan , a retired IDF Major General. Israel Is Our Home Party ( Yisrael Beiteinu ) led by Avigdor Liberman, is also part of Eisenkot’s coalition. Liberman, who formerly held ministerial portfolios in the Israeli government as minister of finance, defense, foreign affairs, strategic affairs, transportation, and national infrastructure alongside being a deputy prime minister, is known for his hawkish stances towards Palestinians. Defending the use of live ammunition by Israeli forces against Palestinian demonstrators during the 2018 Gaza border protests (known as the Great March of Return), Liberman stated : “There are no innocents in Gaza.” Although the components of this coalition are united by their goal to oust Netanyahu, they remain deeply aligned with their political rival’s traditional right-wing stance regarding the Palestinian cause. The coalition opposes the creation of an independent Palestinian state, while supporting the ongoing military operations in the Gaza Strip, the West Bank and other parts of West Asia, and maintaining existing settlement frameworks. Some of the coalition’s affiliated parties further encourage separating Israeli and Palestinian populations, and retaining complete Israeli security control over strategic areas such as the Jordan Valley. They also demand the full demilitarization of any future Palestinian entity. Others call for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority, the annexation of Area C in the West Bank, and the entrenchment of discriminatory policies against Arab citizens in Israel. The Arab-led lists The Arab-led lists represent the minority of Palestinian citizens in Israel (also known as Arab-Israelis), a community that makes up roughly 21% of Israel’s total population, estimated at 10.3 million. Even though both lists fight for the same minority group’s rights, they hold opposing views on the goals, values, and strategy needed to represent them effectively. While representing a minority, these lists hold a critical and often polarizing role in Israeli elections, as they frequently act as a critical balance of power that strongly determines whether a governing coalition can be formed. These lists include the Joint List and the United Arab List. The Joint List The Joint List consists of: The Democratic Front for Peace and Equality ( Hadash ) led by Yousef Jabareen , a prominent Palestinian legal scholar, academic, and politician. The Arab Movement for Renewal ( Ta’al ) led by Dr. Ahmad Tibi , a prominent Palestinian politician, who has served as a member of Knesset since 1999. The National Democratic Alliance ( Balad ) led by a prominent Palestinian politician and historian Sami Abu Shehadeh. The coalition advocates for Palestinian self-determination and civil rights, for an end to the Israeli occupation, and for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state along the 1967 borders with Jerusalem as its capital. It also demands full legal equality and state recognition for Palestinian Arab citizens as an indigenous national minority, and calls for immediate government and law enforcement intervention to curb the increase in organized crime in Arab municipalities. Structural reforms to secure building rights, expand municipal boundaries, and stop punitive home demolitions are top priorities on the Joint List’s agenda. The United Arab List The United Arab List ( Ra’am ) is an Islamist and conservative political party led by Mansour Abbas, a prominent Palestinian politician, whose party was the first independent Arab-Muslim faction to join an Israeli government. Unlike traditional Arab political lists, Ra’am demonstrates a willingness to ally with Jewish political parties in government. It uses a pragmatic, integration-focused strategy to gain political influence and enhance the socioeconomic wellbeing of Arab-Israeli citizens. Ra’am prioritizes the immediate domestic needs of Arab communities inside Israel, such as fighting local organized crime, improving public infrastructure, securing budgets, and resolving housing issues. Netanyahu is alarmed by surging Arab voter turnout Media reports indicated that Arab citizens voted in numbers not seen in decades, which in turn pushed Netanyahu to launch an urgent social media campaign, warning of the growing participation of Arabs. Urging his supporters to go out and vote, Netanyahu appeared in a video , accusing Ra’am of bribing voters with envelopes of cash in the southern areas occupied by Israel. “My brothers and sisters, Likud voters, this is an emergency call, because they are trying to steal the election from us. This morning, the police announced something serious and unusual. They caught three of Ra’am’s senior financial figures with envelopes of cash in the south. This is criminal. They will get to everyone. You have been warned, the voter turnout in the Arab sector in the south is incomparably higher than in the Jewish sector. You must go out and vote,” Netanyahu said. He also claimed that left-wing women escorted Arab women to the polls. Shortly before polls closed at 10:00 pm local time, the final reported voter turnout reached 74.3% , the highest in decades, with exit polls showing no clear winner, and pointing to a political deadlock. It is expected that the final tally and initial results will be published between Thursday afternoon, October 29, and Friday morning, October 30, while the official results will be announced on November 4, 2026. All roads lead to genocide, no matter which bloc wins While many are looking forward to the loss of Netanyahu’s bloc in the elections, hoping that a new government will be less brutal against Palestinians and people across the West Asia region, analysts suggest that Eisenkot’s bloc adopts the same Zionist ethnic cleansing-based ideology. In an interview with BreakThrough News , Israeli-American author, activist and founder of Palestine House of Freedom Miko Peled argued that there are no differences between the two competing blocs when it comes to issues like Israel’s war on Iran, the mass killing in Gaza, forcing Palestinians to flee the besieged enclave. Meanwhile, disputes on the internal Israeli issues – mainly the draft of ultra-orthodox jews in the military and initiating an independent inquiry into the failure of the army and intelligence on the October 7 attacks – remain serious.
